extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers in political economy and public finance
extracted.subtask_description: General principles and practical criteria for designing, levying, and reforming taxes (particularly customs and excise), with examples from 18th-century European states and prescriptive recommendations for improving revenue systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transit duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties imposed on goods carried across a state's territory from one foreign country to another (transit-duties or passage duties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in small states on rivers/straits (example: Danish Sound); often paid entirely by foreigners and may be the only taxes a state can impose on another country's subjects without interfering with its own industry's commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on luxuries: voluntary consumption and unequal incidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes upon luxuries fall on consumers and, because consumption is voluntary, they do not always fall equally or proportionally on individuals' revenues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person's temperament (profuse vs parsimonious) determines contribution more than income; minors or absentees may contribute little or nothing by consumption; this inequality is acceptable insofar as consumption choice is voluntary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty and convenience of taxes on consumables
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes on consumable luxuries can be certain, easily assessed, and convenient in time and mode of payment (paid piece-meal as purchases occur).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When properly assessed on suitable commodities they provoke less grumbling; consumers tend to conflate such taxes with price when merchants advance them; any uncertainty usually arises from poorly worded laws rather than the nature of the duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative cost of consumable taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Levying taxes on consumables often requires many customs/excise officers whose salaries and perquisites are a real cost to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and figures given for Great Britain show varying expense percentages; consolidation of duties (e.g., confining customs to few goods and using excise methods) can reduce collection costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distortion of industry and reduction of productive labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes that raise the price of commodities discourage consumption and thereby reduce production and productive labour, altering the natural direction of national industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: higher foreign wine prices make domestic hardware less valuable to its maker, reducing incentive to produce it; such taxes can shift labour into less advantageous channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smuggling and capital ruin from strict revenue laws
rubrics_metrics.description: High taxes and severe enforcement encourage smuggling, which often leads to forfeitures and penalties that ruin smugglers and absorb productive capital into unproductive uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrupted or wasteful governments provoke public tolerance for smuggling; smuggling breeds perjury and hardened criminality; the capital lost to forfeiture reduces society's productive capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vexation and oppression of dealers by frequent inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Excise-style duties subject dealers to continual visits and examinations by officers, causing significant trouble and vexation (a non-monetary but real cost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excise officers' frequent oversight makes excise duties more unpopular than customs duties, which once paid typically allow merchants respite from further inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of repeated sales taxation (alcavala)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating a duty on every successive sale of goods is highly ruinous to commerce and manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spanish alcavala (tax on every sale) required many officers, inhibited production for distant sale, and is blamed for the ruin of Spanish manufactures and decline of agriculture; lighter or compositional systems (e.g., Naples) are much less harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of taxation promotes free interior commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: A uniform system of taxation across a state reduces internal restraints and lets inland and coasting trade move freely, encouraging prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great Britain's relatively uniform system permits goods to move largely without permits or frequent inspections; extending uniformity to dependent territories would further enhance empire-wide prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm of localized/provincial tax regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Different revenue laws in different provinces multiply the need for revenue officers and severely interrupt interior commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French examples (gabelle, aides, traites, local duties) fragment markets, favor particular provinces (wine favoritism), and require guarding many internal frontiers—hindering national industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct government administration over farming taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes are best levied by an administration whose officers are appointed by government and directly accountable, rather than being farmed to private contractors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farming requires large capital/credit, restricts competition, encourages collusion and exorbitant farmer profits, and adds administrative waste; direct administration can save the farmer's profit and be more frugal and equitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of combining farming with monopoly on necessities
rubrics_metrics.description: When the farmer of a tax also holds a monopoly on a commodity (e.g., salt, tobacco), the people pay both the farmer's rent and monopoly profit—especially injurious when the commodity is a necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salt farms force compulsory purchase and make smuggling irresistible; punishments are severe (galleys, gibbet) yet smuggling persists; such systems yield high revenue but at grave human and social cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of tax law to avoid uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty in what a tax requires or when it is due generally stems from inaccurate or unskillful legislative expression rather than from the nature of the duty itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-drafted, clear statutes reduce disputes and enforcement difficulties; poor wording of law, not the type of tax, causes ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid heavy taxation of necessities to protect manufacturing
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy taxes on the necessaries of life can ruin manufacturers and other productive industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holland's heavy necessities taxation is blamed for industrial decline there; comparatively light British taxes on necessities have not destroyed manufactures—careful tax design on necessities is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of absentees and definitional difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who live abroad (absentees) may derive revenue from a country without contributing by consumption, raising popular calls for taxes on absentees but posing definitional and timing difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxing absentees may be popular (Ireland) but hard to administer: what degree or duration of absence makes one an 'absentee' and when should the tax begin or end?

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform prescriptions for a rational revenue system
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical reform measures include abolishing certain unjust direct taxes (taille, capitation), increasing more equitable taxes (vingtiemes), making indirect taxes uniform across provinces, and placing more taxes under direct government administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such reforms would reduce collection expense, remove vexation on lower ranks, and add farmers' profits to public revenue; political opposition from privileged interests is the main obstacle.
